children.text: I didn't really want to read that because it's 100% AI slop. Even if it's true, it hurts my brain to read it... I just detest the writing style.

From the paper:

> The famous P vs NP problem is a statement about Turing machines. The analogous problem for arithmetic circuits is the VP vs VNP problem. In this paper, we resolve the latter problem, but not the former.

> It has been shown that proving VP = VNP over an appropriate field would imply that P/poly = NP/poly, which is the version of P = NP for Boolean circuits [Bür00b], but no implication in the other direction is known. We show that VP ≠ VNP over all fields, but the P vs NP problem remains open.

For someone who only did a bachelor in informatics, what does this actually mean? What are the ramifications? It's related to P=NP but not quite P=NP?

children.author: CamdenParsons
children.text:
VP: polynomial calculations that have reasonably short recipes using addition and multiplication.

VNP: calculations expressible as sums of potentially enormous numbers of individually easy terms.

VP ≠ VNP: some of those enormous sums cannot be compressed into a short arithmetic recipe, regardless of how clever you are.

children.text:
Some results have been completely unexpected. For example, the refutation of ETH.

And many proofs use existing human ideas in novel, elegant ways — such as disproving the Erdos Unit-Distance Conjecture 80 years after it was posed — AI used clever ideas from algebraic number theory for geometry.

Those AI proofs seem to verify things that are mostly already clear and lack new, human understandable ideas that bring mathematics forward. What exactly is the point besides marketing for AI Labs ? Different perspectives are especially welcome.
